content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue meat, NFS (1167) is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of selected beef cuts marinated in the proprietary NFS sauce and pre‑grilled. The meat has a rich smoky aroma, a slightly sweet flavor, and a tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The NFS (Natural Flavor System) technology uses only natural spices and flavorings without artificial additives.
The meat is marinated for at least 12 hours, allowing deep flavor penetration.
The product undergoes double thermal processing: first marination, then slow smoking at low temperature.
Each portion contains about 150 g of ready‑to‑cook product, convenient for quick meals.
Barbecue meat NFS is popular in fast‑food outlets, cooking shows, and home kitchens.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from beef is highly bioavailable and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and participates in DNA synthesis.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies vitamins B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Barbecue meat fits well into low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no carbs.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The marinade contains salt; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Thermal handling
items.content: Improper reheating can allow bacterial growth; follow storage and heating instructions.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The product contains saturated fats; those with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Barbecue meat can be reheated in the microwave (1–2 minutes) or on a skillet (2–3 minutes per side). It works well in sandwiches, salads, tacos, pasta dishes, or served as a main course with a side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging and consume within 5 days after opening. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Ensure the meat is fully heated before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Black beans are small, glossy, black-skinned seeds of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), native to the Americas. They have a creamy interior and a mild, earthy, slightly sweet flavor. Black beans are a staple in Latin American, Caribbean, and Southwestern cuisines and are eaten in soups, stews, rice dishes, tacos, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans belong to the same species as kidney beans, pinto beans, and navy beans.
They have been cultivated in the Americas for thousands of years.
Black beans are the main ingredient in dishes such as feijoada and black bean soup.
Their dark color comes from anthocyanins, plant pigments found in the seed coat.
The cooking liquid of black beans is often kept as part of the dish because it is flavorful.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Black beans provide protein, making them a staple in many plant-based diets.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Black beans are high in fiber, which supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides folate, iron, and magnesium
items.content: These nutrients support cell function, oxygen transport, and muscle function.

items.title: Contains anthocyanins
items.content: These plant pigments have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Slow-digesting carbohydrates
items.content: Black beans have a relatively low glycemic index and contain resistant starch.

items.title: Must be thoroughly cooked
items.content: Raw or undercooked beans contain lectins that can cause nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Soak dried beans, discard the soaking water, and boil them thoroughly.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Black beans contain fermentable carbohydrates that may cause gas or bloating in some people.

items.title: Sodium in canned products
items.content: Canned black beans can be high in added salt, so rinse them and check labels.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Bean allergy is uncommon but can occur, and some people allergic to other legumes may also react.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black beans can be soaked and simmered until tender, then added to soups, stews, burritos, tacos, salads, and rice dishes, or mashed into dips and burgers. Canned black beans should be rinsed before use. Pair them with rice for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried black beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, where they keep for a year or longer. Cooked black beans should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days, or frozen for longer storage. Unopened canned beans can be stored in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans and rice is a popular fast‑food dish consisting of boiled pinto beans mixed with fluffy white rice. It is usually served hot, sometimes topped with spices, sauce, or cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pinto beans originated in Mexico and are among the most nutritious legumes.
The bean‑and‑rice combination provides a complete set of essential amino acids, making it a full‑protein meal.
In the United States the dish is often offered at chain fast‑food restaurants as an inexpensive lunch option.
Pinto beans are rich in antioxidants, especially polyphenols, which give them their characteristic reddish hue.
Traditionally the rice is steamed to keep it light and separate from the beans.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Pinto beans contain about 21 g of protein per 100 g, and rice adds complementary amino acids, enhancing protein quality.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The dish fits well into low‑fat diets when not paired with heavy sauces.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans before cooking lowers its level.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: People monitoring blood sugar may prefer whole‑grain or brown rice instead of white rice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, often in a disposable container. It can be topped with salsa, guacamole, shredded cheese, or fresh vegetables for added flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It freezes well for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before eating.

potato-salad-made-with-light-mayonnaise-.title: Potato Salad with Light Mayonnaise Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad made with a light mayonnaise-type dressing is a classic dish where boiled potatoes are tossed with a gentle, low‑fat mayo‑based sauce. It is popular as a side dish or a light meal, especially during warm weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In many countries the salad is a staple at picnics and family gatherings.
Light mayonnaise dressing contains fewer fats and calories than regular mayo, often using reduced‑fat oil or yogurt.
The salad is commonly garnished with fresh herbs such as dill or parsley and finely chopped onion.
Some regional variations add boiled eggs, pickles, or a touch of mustard for extra flavor.
Potato salad keeps well in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The salad retains vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, a mineral that aids blood‑pressure regulation and heart health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using a light mayo reduces saturated fat content, making the dish more suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If the potato skins are left on, the salad adds dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional mayo contains eggs; people with egg allergy should use an egg‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excess salt in the dressing can raise blood pressure; monitor added salt.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Leaving the salad at room temperature for more than 2 hours can allow bacterial proliferation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even a light dressing adds calories; portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side to meat, fish, or as a light standalone meal. Garnish with herbs, sliced boiled eggs, or olives for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Consume within 3‑4 days. Stir before serving as the dressing may settle.
